analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $6.50 an hour.
analysis.headline: A bill to raise the federal minimum wage to $6.50 an hour was introduced in August 1992 and died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to lift the federal minimum wage from $4.25 an hour to $6.50 an hour, with the new rate taking effect 90 days after enactment [S2] [S3]. It was introduced late in the 102nd Congress by Rep. Martin Sabo, referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, then sent to a subcommittee, and never advanced further before Congress ended [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum wage would get a $2.25-an-hour raise, a roughly 53% increase, starting 90 days after the bill became law [S3]. Their families and anyone whose wages are tied to the minimum wage would also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the $4.25 minimum wage with a $6.50 floor, effective 90 days after enactment [S3].
The raise is roughly 53% above the existing $4.25 rate [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay at or near the minimum wage — restaurants, retail stores, and other low-wage businesses — would bear higher payroll costs, and some of that cost could be passed to consumers in higher prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers like restaurants and retail

drawbacks.text: Employers facing a 53% jump in their wage floor would pay more in labor costs, which economists often warn can mean fewer entry-level jobs, reduced hours, or higher prices for customers.
The bill gives employers no phase-in period beyond 90 days and no regional cost-of-living adjustment, so businesses in low-cost areas would absorb the same wage floor as those in high-cost cities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would put substantially more money in the pockets of the country's lowest-paid workers, at a real cost to low-wage employers. The abrupt 90-day jump and lack of phase-in make it a blunt instrument, but the core effect — a large raise for minimum wage workers — is straightforward.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to a subcommittee, and Congress ended before it ever reached the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Martin Sabo introduced the bill on August 12, 1992, late in the second session of the 102nd Congress [S1] [S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S5].
On October 9, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, where it remained until Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].
No vote, hearing, or further action is recorded in the bill's history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that pay minimum wage kept the $4.25 wage floor instead of facing a $6.50 rate, so their payroll costs stayed lower. Minimum wage workers missed the raise.

for.name: Rep. Martin Olav Sabo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the minimum wage to $6.50 an hour

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Took no further action on the bill after receiving the referral; it was passed to a subcommittee and never brought back for a markup or floor vote

against.name: House Subcommittee on Labor Standards
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on October 9, 1992, and never acted on it before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican support is recorded, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: These employers are among the largest users of the minimum wage and would face a 53% increase in their wage floor. Their interest in stopping the bill ran directly against the interests of minimum wage workers.
Any business paying at or near $4.25 an hour would face higher payroll costs under the bill. Blocking it preserved their current cost structure at workers' expense.
